newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - LVMH to buy U.S. duty free firm.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - LVMH to buy U.S. duty free firm.

text.p: French luxury goods flagship LVMH said on Wednesday it planned to buy U.S. duty free chain DFS for 12.6 billion francs ($2.5 billion), boosting its presence along the affluent Pacific rim and extending control over its sales.

The company said in a statement that it had struck a deal to acquire 59 percent of San Francisco-based DFS, which it described as the world's No. 1 distributor of luxury goods through 180 boutiques at airports and city centres.

The deal marks LVMH's first major foray into the retail sector. The French group, best known for its Moet & Chandon champagnes, Hennessy cognacs, Christian Dior perfumes and Louis Vuitton designer luggage, has focused until recently on small brand acquisitions such as luxury leather goods firm Celine.

Investors applauded the deal, driving up the share price more than three percent up, but credit rating agency Standard & Poor's cautioned that the sizeable acquisition risked marring LVMH's pristine balance sheet.
Shares in LVMH, one of the bluest chips on the Paris bourse, closed up 3.41 percent at 1,153 francs, off their session highs of 1,172.
"Thanks to this acquisition, LVMH will increase its presence in the Asia-Pacific region and emerging countries, a future growth area," it said in a statement.
The company said DFS had annual sales of more than 15 billion francs and 20 years' experience in retailing in Asia.
The rapidly-growing Asia-Pacific region is a key market for LVMH, which generated 54 percent of its 1995 sales of 29.8 billion francs in the United States and the Far East.
"This deal has fabulous development potential for us. It's a diversification that's linked directly to our business," a company spokeswoman told Reuters.

The company's retail experience up to now has been largely confined to the elegant Paris department store Bon Marche, owned by one of the LVMH holding companies controlled by chairman Bernard Arnault.
LVMH said it would keep DFS's management team in place and that the chain would be managed independently from its other luxury goods businesses.
"It's a very good deal," said one trader, citing the importance of the Pacific Rim region for the group given the weak spending climate in Europe.

But S&P said it may downgrade its rating on LVMH short-term paper, currently rated A-1+. It said the acquisition of DFS would increase the group's control over the distribution of its products, but would massively increase its debt.
"Its pro forma net financial debt would rise to around 16 billion francs from around 3.1 billion francs on June 30, 1996," it said in a statement.
"The flexibility that LVMH had, reflecting low debt that was comfortably covered by cashflow, risks being reduced," it said. LVMH's cashflow last year was 5.9 billion francs last year.
LVMH said the acquisition of 58.75 percent of DFS hinged on certain conditions but declined to elaborate pending a finalisation of the deal.
Industry sources said LVMH is waiting for a resolution of a dispute among DFS's owners that is being handled by a U.S. mediator. But they said LVMH had clinched an agreement with the majority.

The New York Times reported on Wednesday that billionaire Robert Miller, who owns 38.75 percent of the DFS duty-free store empire, was trying to block a sale by his partners. It reported Miller said the deal would violate the terms of an agreement he signed in 1991 with his partners.
